children: The Netherlands has moved around 86 tonnes of gold from the US and Canada to London, citing rising geopolitical risks and the need to ensure its reserves can be deployed quickly in a crisis. The move has put a spotlight on a question that central banks are increasingly having to consider: where should they keep their gold?

Between March and August 2026, De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) transferred approximately 86 tonnes of gold from New York and Ottawa to London. The amount represented about 27.5% of the roughly 313 tonnes it had previously held across the US and Canada.
"In view of increasing geopolitical unrest, DNB is strengthening its crisis preparedness," the Dutch central bank said.

The reason for choosing London is largely about liquidity. DNB said gold held at the Bank of England has to meet modern international trading standards and is regarded as "the world's most easily tradable gold". That makes it easier to mobilise in an emergency.
"The gold reserves held in New York and Ottawa cannot be utilised as quickly and directly in such a situation," DNB said.
DNB Governor Olaf Sleijpen said the move was not about expecting an immediate crisis, but about being prepared for one.

"With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves. We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," Sleijpen said.
How much gold does the Netherlands hold?

The Netherlands has 612.4 tonnes of gold reserves, worth around 72.2 billion euros ($83.6 billion) at the end of 2025. The reserves are spread across DNB's Cash Centre in Zeist and central-bank facilities in London, New York and Ottawa.

The relocation has significantly changed that distribution. London's share has risen from 18.1% to 32.1%, making it the largest overseas location. New York's share has fallen from 31.3% to 18.5%, while Ottawa's has declined from 19.7% to 18.5%. Zeist continues to hold 30.8%.

The move was also not simply a matter of loading 86 tonnes onto trucks and aircraft. DNB sold approximately 59 tonnes in New York and bought an equivalent amount in London. More than 27 tonnes was physically moved from North America to Zeist, while a similar quantity was subsequently moved from Zeist to London.

"Combining the processes of buying and selling and physical transport has allowed DNB to spread the risks associated with such a complex physical gold relocation operation, while also ensuring efficiency and cost-consciousness," DNB said.
Is this a vote of no confidence in the US?
DNB has not described the move as politically motivated. Instead, it has repeatedly framed it as risk diversification and crisis planning.

But the timing is significant. Global trade tensions, wars, sanctions and concerns about the safety of sovereign assets held overseas have made the location of central-bank reserves a more important consideration.
Laurent Schwartz, president of the Paris-based National Gold Counter, said central banks have been moving their reserves for about a decade.
"The current political context in the United States might also push certain central banks into favouring other storage locations," he said.
Schwartz described London as the deepest and most liquid gold market, making bullion easier to deploy during a crisis.
"Central banks can more easily lend their gold there to other banking institutions."
John Plassard, an analyst at Cite Gestion Private Bank, said the Dutch move was intended "for there to be more immediate availability in the event of a crisis".
For now, he called it a "fairly one-off move". But Plassard warned that if other central banks followed the Netherlands, it could damage confidence in the US.
Is this part of a bigger gold rethink?

The Netherlands is not the first European country to reconsider where its bullion is stored. France moved 129 tonnes of gold from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York back to France between 2025 and 2026, while Germany previously repatriated more than 600 tonnes from New York to Frankfurt.
That does not necessarily mean central banks are abandoning US vaults. Germany, for instance, continues to regard the New York Fed as an important storage location.

But the Dutch move highlights a broader shift in thinking. Gold is not merely a reserve that central banks want to accumulate; they also want to ensure that it can be accessed, traded and deployed when financial or geopolitical conditions deteriorate.
DNB itself summed up the logic behind the move by describing gold as "the ultimate reserve asset" because it can hedge extreme systemic risks.
"Keeping a larger share of the gold reserves in London strengthens the function of gold as an anchor of trust," DNB said.

title: 86 tonnes of Dutch gold moved out of US vaults. What is the Netherlands bracing for?
